newsitem.title: DUBAI: Korean car sales rise in Gulf at Japanese expense.
newsitem.headline: Korean car sales rise in Gulf at Japanese expense.

text.p: Passenger car sales in Gulf Arab states are declining, with Japanese models suffering most and Korean makes forging ahead at their expense, a report by Emirates Industrial Bank (EIB) said on Monday.
"Since 1993, passenger car sales have been falling for all kinds of vehicles," the United Arab Emirates' bank said in the February issue of its journal.

"Japanese makes suffered the most as their prices rose the most because of the long-term strengthening of the yen," it said. "In 1995 alone, prices of Japanese cars rose by around 20 percent compared to 1994."
The journal said the market share of Japanese cars dropped from 75 percent in the late 1980s to a current 55 percent.
It said the most remarkable event of the market slump was the entry and consolidation of Korean makes.

"From a position of virtual insignificance, Korea now ranks third among automobile suppliers to the Gulf -- after Japan and the United States respectively -- commanding a sizeable almost 10 percent of the passenger car market," the journal said.
U.S. cars hold a market share of about 25 percent.
Korean cars had managed to make inroads where others fell behind thanks to its strategy of offering inexpensive cars backed by good distributor support, it said.
A recent increase in demand for compact, cheaper cars had suited Korean manufacturers, which offered cars at prices up to 20 percent below comparative Japanese models, the journal said.

"The Koreans are likely to replace the Japanese in the lower segment, which is going to be largely determined by their ability and capacity to meet the demand. Other segments are expected to remain stable," it said.
The bank's journal said there was little sign of any significant recovery in the Gulf automobile market -- which had boomed in the early 1990s -- saying the upward pressure on prices would continue.
